opus-5.5.text:
I think the progress in coding has been surprisingly fast, even for people working on it. A few years ago models could autocomplete a line or write a small function, and that already felt magical. Then quite quickly we got to models that could solve competitive programming problems, then fix real bugs in real repositories, and now they're increasingly able to take on longer tasks: reading a codebase, making a plan, editing many files, running tests, and iterating.

Coding moved faster than many other domains largely because it has a very good feedback signal. You can run the code. You can check whether the tests pass. That makes it much easier to train with reinforcement learning, because you have something close to a verifiable reward. Combine that with huge amounts of code data and the fact that researchers are themselves programmers who care a lot about this use case, and you get a domain where every ingredient lines up.

On the timeline, I'd think of it less as one jump and more as the length and complexity of tasks the model can handle on its own keeps stretching: from seconds of work, to minutes, to hours. The interesting question now is less "can it write correct code" and more "can it work like a real engineer over a long horizon": understand vague requirements, keep context, recover from its own mistakes, and know when to ask a human.

I'm cautious about giving precise dates, because predictions here have been wrong in both directions. But I'd say the trend is quite steady. Software engineering will probably be one of the first professions where AI changes day-to-day work in a deep way. Over time, a lot of the job will shift from writing code to specifying what you want, reviewing, and making judgment calls about design and trade-offs. Those parts, taste and understanding what's actually worth building, are harder to automate, and I think they'll matter even more.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes rapid progress from autocomplete to longer coding tasks, but does not state that this progress has continued since Claude 3.5 New.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's gone faster than almost anyone inside the field expected, and I include myself in that.

If you go back to 2022, when I was working on ReAct and later SWE-bench with my collaborators at Princeton, the models could barely do a single-file bug fix reliably. SWE-bench was designed to be hard precisely because real GitHub issues require you to navigate a codebase, understand context, and make a change that passes tests. The first numbers were in the low single digits. We thought that benchmark would last years.

It didn't. Within about eighteen months you had agentic systems solving a large fraction of those tasks, and the pace since then has been more like a compounding curve than a linear one. I think the key shift was that people stopped treating coding as a text-generation problem and started treating it as a reasoning-and-acting problem. Once you give the model a loop, let it run tests, read errors, and iterate, the ceiling moves dramatically. That's the thing I care about most: language agents that can take actions in an environment, not just produce a plausible answer.

So how do I see the timeline going forward? I'd break it into a few phases. The first phase, which we're largely through, is autocomplete and single-function help. The second phase, which is now, is task-level autonomy: you describe an issue and the agent handles the whole thing end to end, maybe with you reviewing a pull request. The third phase, which I think is coming within a couple of years rather than a decade, is project-level autonomy, where the agent owns a subsystem over days or weeks, makes architectural choices, and asks you questions when it's actually uncertain rather than when it's confused.

The bottleneck in that third phase is not raw intelligence. It's evaluation and feedback. Coding happens to be the domain where we have the best reward signals available: tests pass or they don't, code compiles or it doesn't. That's why coding is leading everything else. Other domains will follow, but more slowly, because the signals are murkier.

The one thing I'd caution against is reading benchmark saturation as "solved." Every time a benchmark saturates, it's partly because the models got better and partly because the benchmark stopped measuring what matters. The real test is whether an engineer at a company trusts the agent with something they'd be embarrassed to get wrong. We're closer to that than people think, but we're not there yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid progress from 2022 onward, but it does not mention Claude 3.5 New or state that progress has been sustained since that release.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by coding capabilities. If we mean solving a well-defined problem—here’s the specification, here are the tests—that can improve very quickly. But if we mean taking responsibility for a software project, the timeline is harder to predict.

In real software engineering, a lot of the work is figuring out what should be built, understanding an existing codebase, and checking whether a change actually solves the user’s problem. Writing the code is only part of that. A system can be very good at producing a patch and still need a lot of supervision over a longer task.

So I would look less at a particular date and more at how long an AI can work independently before someone needs to intervene. Can it finish a small task? Can it handle a project that takes several days, including debugging and responding to feedback? As that reliable working horizon grows, the impact becomes much larger.

I expect rapid progress to continue, but I’m more confident about the direction than the exact timeline. The important transition is from helping a person write code to being able to own a task and verify that it’s done.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects rapid progress to continue but does not say it has been sustained since Claude 3.5 New.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate two questions: when AI can write code well, and when it can take responsibility for an entire software engineering task. Those can have quite different timelines.

Writing a function with a clear specification is relatively easy to evaluate. But in real software engineering, you have to figure out what the user wants, understand an existing repository, make changes, run tests, and respond when something breaks. The challenge becomes maintaining useful progress over a long sequence of actions.

So I expect progress to be rapid, but uneven. We may see systems that are very strong on well-defined tasks while still needing substantial supervision on ambiguous projects. Better models will help, but so will better tools, environments, and feedback.

I’m more comfortable predicting that the amount of work we can delegate will grow than giving a specific year when coding is ‘solved.’ The important question is how long a system can work independently before a human needs to intervene—and whether the result actually meets the user’s needs.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts rapid but uneven future progress, but does not state that AI coding capabilities have made sustained rapid progress since Claude 3.5 New.
